title: Subdomain takeover: `candle-src.etoro.com` CNAME points at a deleted Azure Traffic Manager profile
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

`candle-src.etoro.com` — an in-scope etoro.com hostname — still carries a CNAME to an Azure Traffic
Manager profile that no longer exists:

```
candle-src.etoro.com.  60  IN  CNAME  prod-candle.trafficmanager.net.
```

`prod-candle.trafficmanager.net` returns `NXDOMAIN` (no A, no CNAME, no SOA of its own), and
`https://candle-src.etoro.com/` fails at the TLS stage because nothing in the chain answers.

A Traffic Manager profile's DNS label is only unique while the profile exists. Once the profile is
deleted the label `prod-candle` is released to any Azure subscription that creates a profile with that
name, and because eToro's own record still points at it, the attacker never has to touch eToro DNS:
creating the profile and attaching an External endpoint makes `candle-src.etoro.com` resolve to
attacker-controlled infrastructure. The label is guessable from the hostname itself.

## Scope

This report is filed against structured scope `candle-src.etoro.com` (id 18313, bounty-eligible,
programme maximum severity critical). The wildcard `*.etoro.com` also covers the hostname.

## Steps to reproduce

1. `dig +short CNAME candle-src.etoro.com`
   → `prod-candle.trafficmanager.net.`
2. `dig +short A prod-candle.trafficmanager.net`
   → empty
3. `dig prod-candle.trafficmanager.net` → `status: NXDOMAIN`
4. `curl -sS https://candle-src.etoro.com/` → connection fails without a TLS response
   (curl exit 6, HTTP code 000)

Verification date: 2026-11-03. NXDOMAIN on the *label itself* is what distinguishes a deleted profile
from a merely unhealthy one — an existing profile always answers for its endpoints.

## Why it is exploitable

1. Create a Traffic Manager profile named `prod-candle` in an Azure subscription you control.
2. Add an External endpoint pointing at a host you control.
3. `candle-src.etoro.com` now resolves to your endpoint, over eToro-branded DNS.
4. Request a certificate for `candle-src.etoro.com` (ACME HTTP-01 validates against content you serve),
   so the site presents a valid certificate and no browser warning.

## Remediation

Delete the A/CNAME for `candle-src.etoro.com`, or recreate the `prod-candle` Traffic Manager profile in
a subscription eToro controls and keep it for the lifetime of the record. Sweep the zone for other
CNAMEs whose targets no longer resolve — this record was found in a passive sweep of paying-scope
zones, and the same class of record is easy to miss because the hostname is not linked from any page.

## What was and was not done

Passive DNS resolution only: public DNS lookups and a single unauthenticated GET of the hostname.
No Azure profile was created, no name was reserved, no account was registered on any target, and no
other in-scope asset was touched. The claim path was deliberately not exercised — reserving the label
would itself be a takeover of a production name, which is the vendor's call to make.
impact:
Any content served from `candle-src.etoro.com` — phishing, credential capture, malware — carries
eToro's brand on a hostname inside the etoro.com zone, with a certificate the attacker can legitimately
obtain, so there is no browser warning and no visible difference from an eToro site.

Because the hostname sits under the same parent domain, cookies scoped to `.etoro.com` become reachable
from attacker-controlled content, and any allow-list or CSP `script-src` entry that trusts `*.etoro.com`
is bypassed.

Integrations, historical client builds and QA configuration that still call `candle-src.etoro.com`
silently talk to the attacker instead of eToro, which is a supply-chain path into those environments.

Severity: CVSS 4.0 `AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:L/VI:L/SC:L/SI:L/SL:L/SA:N` = 6.9 (medium). The CVSS 3.1
equivalent with a scope change is 7.2; the takeover is unauthenticated and needs no user interaction.
